title: Star clusters: open, globular, and the age at the turn-off
intro_sentence: A star cluster is a family of stars born together from one cloud of gas. Because its stars share an age and a distance, a cluster shows stars of different masses ageing side by side, and tells how old the whole group is.
body_paragraphs: The stars of a cluster formed at almost the same time from the same cloud, so they have the same age and nearly the same chemical make-up, and they lie at about the same distance from us. What differs between them is mainly their mass. That makes a cluster a natural experiment in how stars live. Astronomers sort clusters into two kinds that differ in almost every way: loose, mostly young open clusters in the galaxy's disc, and dense, ancient globular clusters, mostly in its halo.

An open cluster holds tens to thousands of stars, with a core a few light-years across and a looser outer part tens of light-years wide. Open clusters lie in the disc of the Milky Way, in and between the spiral arms, and most are less than a billion years old: they are only weakly bound, and tidal forces from the galaxy, encounters with gas clouds and the slow loss of their own stars gradually disperse them. The Hyades, about 153 light-years away and 600 to 700 million years old, is the nearest star cluster to the Sun. The Pleiades, about 445 light-years away, is younger, a little over 100 million years. The Beehive (M44), about 600 light-years away, is about as old as the Hyades, and M67, about 2,700 to 2,800 light-years away, is about 4 billion years old, close to the Sun's age and the oldest open cluster in the Messier catalogue. A 2023 search of the Gaia satellite's data recovered about 7,200 clusters and candidates in our galaxy; only 134 of them are globular clusters.

A globular cluster is a dense ball of tens of thousands to millions of stars, 50 to 450 light-years across. The Milky Way has about 150 of them, spread mostly through its halo, and their stars are about 8 to 13 billion years old, among the oldest in the galaxy. Omega Centauri (NGC 5139), about 17,700 light-years away, is the largest and brightest in the sky, with about 10 million stars and about ten times the mass of other big globular clusters; it may be the leftover core of a small galaxy that the Milky Way stripped of its outer stars. In 2024, Hubble measurements of seven fast-moving stars near its centre gave strong evidence for an intermediate-mass black hole of at least 8,200 solar masses there. 47 Tucanae (NGC 104), about 15,000 light-years away, is the second brightest, and M13 in Hercules, about 24,000 light-years away with more than 100,000 stars, was the target of the radio message sent from the Arecibo telescope in 1974.

A cluster's age is read from its turn-off. On the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, most of its stars fall on the main sequence, where stars fuse hydrogen in their cores. More massive stars use up their fuel faster: the Sun will spend about 10 billion years on the main sequence, the most massive stars only millions. So as a cluster ages, its main sequence is used up from the top: the most massive, brightest and bluest stars leave it first. The point where what is left of the main sequence bends away towards the giants, the main-sequence turn-off, marks the stars that are just running out of hydrogen in their cores; their lifetime is about the cluster's age, and the turn-off moves down to fainter, less massive stars as the cluster grows older. A few stars sit above the turn-off and look too young: blue stragglers, probably made when a star pulled fresh hydrogen from a companion or two stars merged. A 2020 study of 68 globular clusters put the average age of the oldest at about 13.3 billion years, give or take half a billion. The universe must be older than its oldest stars, and the same study estimated its age at about 13.5 billion years.
diagram_caption: Open clusters: young, loose, in the disc. Globular clusters: old, dense, in the halo. The main-sequence turn-off moves to fainter stars as a cluster ages, and gives its age.
